deals.atTheTable: P–P–1♦–P–1♥–(1♠)–2♦–(2♠)–3♦, all pass. 3♦ made 11 tricks (+150, 3 of 9). Five tables bid 5♦ for +400 or +420.
deals.agreed: West's 2♦ showed a minimum (12-15); with 16 HCP, a strong six-card suit and five losers, West jumps to 3♦ (16-18, six diamonds), invitational even after the overcall. East, a passed hand with a maximum and four trumps, then bids 5♦ (no spade stopper for 3NT). Agreed by Dave, 2026-11-16.
reviewNotes: Double dummy, East-West make 11 tricks in diamonds and only 8 in notrump. Par is 5♦= (+400).
North's call over 3♦ is a guess: at the table North bid 2♠ over 2♦ with K9854 and 8 HCP, so North might bid 3♠ here. East would still bid 5♦.
East's decision at the table, after 2♦–(2♠), was also discussed: a 3♠ cuebid (over 10 points and a fit) or 4♦, not 3♦. It isn't drilled here, because the agreed auction goes differently.
Tagged opener-rebids, a new topic for opener's second bid (2026-11-16).

problems.explanation: Count your hand: 16 HCP, a strong six-card diamond suit, a side four-card club suit and a singleton spade, about five losers. That's much better than a minimum. A simple 2♦ rebid shows 12-15, so jump to 3♦: 16-18 with a good six-card suit, inviting game. The overcall doesn't change that. Partner, with a fit and a maximum, can now bid 5♦.

whyNot.2D: The call made at the table. It shows a minimum, 12-15, so partner, a passed hand, could only compete to 3♦, and you stopped there (+150, 3 of 9). 5♦ makes.
whyNot.2C: A new suit at the two level, but it's not forcing and doesn't show your extra strength or the six-card diamond suit.

deals.atTheTable: 1♣–(1♥)–1NT–(P)–2♣–(2♥), all pass. 2♥ went one down (+50, 4 of 9). One table made 3NT for +600.
deals.agreed: West, with a maximum 1NT response (10 HCP) and KJ64 of hearts, bids 2NT. It tells partner definitively that West has a heart stopper and is at the top of the 6-10 range. Partner opened and rebid clubs, so there are 22+ HCP between us and partner has five or six clubs; with their suit stopped, notrump is likely a better spot than clubs. Not a double: Donna would probably read it as takeout, showing spades and diamonds. Agreed by Dave and Donna, 2026-11-16.
reviewNotes: Double dummy, East-West make 9 tricks in notrump (3NT +600, a top) and only 7 in clubs; 2♥ by South makes only 6 tricks, so doubled it's two down (+300, about 8 of 9).
Par is a North–South save in 4♦ doubled, two down (−300), but North never mentioned diamonds and hardly any table got there.
East's 3NT over 2NT is a judgment: 13 HCP, six clubs and the heart AQ make it reasonable, and it makes double dummy.

The double's meaning isn't formally agreed, but Donna thinks she'd read it as takeout (spades and diamonds), so it's a whyNot, not acceptable (2026-11-16). See 'Penalty or takeout doubles' under discussion in agreements.md.
Tagged general: no existing topic fits.

problems.explanation: Your 1NT showed about 6-10 with a heart stopper, and you have the top of the range: 10 HCP with KJ64 of hearts sitting over the heart bidder. Partner opened and rebid clubs, so you have 22+ HCP between you and partner has five or six clubs. Don't sell out to 2♥: bid 2NT. It tells partner for certain that you have hearts stopped and a maximum, and invites 3NT. With their suit stopped and no fit of your own, notrump is likely to play better than clubs. Partner, with a good hand, bids 3NT.

whyNot.X: Meant as penalty, it would score well (2♥ doubled is two down double dummy, +300). But partner would probably read it as takeout: 'I have spades and diamonds, bid one of them.' 2NT says what you have without the risk.
whyNot.P: The call made at the table. It sells out cheaply when you have a maximum and their suit stopped (+50, 4 of 9). Be aggressive below 2NT.
whyNot.3C: It competes, but with your heart stopper and only two clubs, notrump is the better destination. Double dummy 3♣ makes only seven tricks.

deals.atTheTable: (P)–1♦–(P)–2♣–(P)–2NT, all pass. West meant 2NT as 18-19, as after a one-level response; East read it as a minimum and passed. 2NT made nine tricks (+150, 1 of 9). The field bid 4♠ or 3NT for +620 to +690.
deals.agreed: East, with 9 HCP, four spades and six clubs, responds 1♠: too weak for a two-level response (10+), and with less than an opening hand responder shows a four-card major at the one level first. West, with 19 and four spades, raises to 4♠. Agreed by Dave, 2026-11-17.
reviewNotes: Double dummy, East-West make 10 tricks in notrump, spades and clubs, and 9 in hearts. Par is 3NT+1 (+630); 4♠= is +620.
One of two versions of this board, sharing its source: this one drills East's response and West's raise; the other drills West's rebid after East's 2♣, as at the table.

problems.explanation: Partner opened 1♦. You have 9 HCP, four spades and six clubs. A two-level response like 2♣ promises 10+, and with less than an opening hand you show a four-card major at the one level first: bid 1♠. It's forcing for one round, so you can show the clubs later, and it finds a spade fit at once.

whyNot.2C: The call made at the table. A two-level response promises 10+, and you have 9. It also hides your spades: partner will take 2♣ as denying a four-card major.
whyNot.1N: 1NT denies a four-card major. With four spades, bid them.
whyNot.3C: A jump shift shows a strong hand, about 17+. You have 9.

problems.explanation: Partner's 1♠ shows four or more spades and 6+ points, and you have four spades too: a 4-4 fit. With 19 HCP you have game opposite even a minimum response, so raise straight to 4♠.

whyNot.3S: A jump raise shows about 16-18 and only invites: partner passes with a minimum. With 19, bid the game.
whyNot.2N: A jump to 2NT shows 18-19 balanced, but you've found a 4-4 spade fit. Tell partner: 4♠.

deals.atTheTable: (P)–1♦–(P)–2♣–(P)–2NT, all pass. West meant 2NT as 18-19, as after a one-level response; East read it as a minimum and passed. 2NT made nine tricks (+150, 1 of 9). The field bid 4♠ or 3NT for +620 to +690.
deals.agreed: After a two-level response, 2NT shows a minimum (12-14) and 3NT 15-18, so with 19 West must not rebid 2NT. East's 2♣ most likely denies a four-card major (with less than an opening hand, responder bids the major at the one level), so West bids 3NT. 2♥ (forcing, since 2♣ promised another bid) or a 3♥ jump shift is also fine. Agreed by Dave, 2026-11-16; revised 2026-11-17.
reviewNotes: Double dummy, East-West make 10 tricks in notrump, spades and clubs, and 9 in hearts. Par is 3NT+1 (+630); 4♠= is +620.
One of two versions of this board, sharing its source: this one drills West's rebid after East's 2♣, as at the table; the other drills East's 1♠ response and West's raise.

problems.explanation: You planned to open and rebid 2NT to show 18-19 balanced, but that works only after a one-level response. Partner's 2♣ is a two-level response, promising 10+, so you have at least 29 between you and game is certain. Now 2NT would show a minimum, 12-14, and partner may pass it. With less than an opening hand, partner would have shown a four-card major at the one level, so 2♣ most likely denies one: bid 3NT. If partner has more, partner can bid on.

acceptable.2H: A new suit, forcing because 2♣ promised another bid. It finds a 4-4 fit if partner has an opening hand and a major to show later, but 2♣ most likely denies one.
acceptable.3H: A jump shift, forcing to game. Fine, but it uses up room, and 2♣ most likely denies a major.

whyNot.2N: The call made at the table. After a two-level response, 2NT shows a minimum (12-14), and partner passed (+150, 1 of 9). 18-19 balanced is a jump to 2NT only after a one-level response.
